en: The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Candraprabha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Dharma-bhadra, Imperial Subject and Grand Master of Illuminating Teaching,
Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, under Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, preaching the Dharma to a great assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana went before the Buddha; having prostrated themselves on the ground with their five limbs touching the earth and paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We cannot bear to see the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa; therefore, at this very moment, we shall first enter extinction.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly who joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition do Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana now wish to enter parinirvāṇa before the Buddha?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will resolve the doubts of the assembly.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you."

Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana have exhausted all outflows, including greed, hatred, and delusion; they have accomplished what was to be done, established the holy life, and will not undergo further existence. It is not only today that they first desire to enter parinirvāṇa.
In the past, within North India, there was a great city named Bhadraśilā, twelve yojanas in length and equally broad in width.

There was a king there named Candraprabha, whose lifespan was forty thousand years; he possessed the divine eye and the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). His physical form was upright and majestic, endowed with all the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and his radiance shone forth like the full moon in heaven.
Wherever he went, he required no illumination from lamps, candles, the sun, or the moon; therefore, he was called Candraprabha.
He ruled over the four continents and sixty-eight thousand kingdoms.

At that time, the world was abundant and the people were peaceful and secure; gold, silver, precious gems, food, drink, clothing, and vehicles—including elephants, horses, and carriages—were all present in full abundance.
At each of the four gates of the city there were multi-storied pavilions, with doors, windows, and balconies all adorned with various precious gems;
the streets, lanes, and alleys were swept clean and sprinkled with water, and banners, streamers, jeweled canopies, and pearl necklaces were erected throughout.

Furthermore, there were fragrances of agallochum, powdered incense, and sandalwood; whenever a gentle breeze arose, it wafted these scents throughout the city and its environs, so that neither those in carriages, nor horsemen, nor passers-by could smell any foul odors.

In various places there were also flowering and fruit-bearing trees—the *tāmarasa* tree, the *karnikāra* tree, the *nīpa* tree, the *pāṭala* tree, the *sāla* tree, the *tilaka* tree, the *nāgapuṣpa* tree, the *mucilinda* tree, the *atimuktaka* tree, and the *bhaṭṭāra* tree—all of which were luxuriant and flourishing.
Parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, koyaṣṭikas, and other such birds produced exquisite sounds among the trees.
Within and without the city, flowing springs and bathing pools constantly yielded beautiful flowers—blue lotuses (utpala), water lilies (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka).
"Such was his wealth and honor, with all manner of adornments.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the Devaputra Candraprabha gathered gold, silver, precious gems, elephants, horses, chariots, food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and various other articles of adornment at the marketplaces, streets, and the four gates of the city. He then struck a golden drum and proclaimed to the multitude:"
"Prince Candraprabha universally bestows all kinds of wealth and goods upon all beings.
Whatever they require according to their wishes, he provides to those who seek it.

At that time, all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa came to the royal city to request what was given; there were none who did not receive abundance, and they attained great wealth and status, such that there was not a single person left in poverty or living as a mendicant.
At that time, the Devaputra Candraprabha further reflected to himself:
"Although all sentient beings lack nothing, their resources still do not equal my own."
Furthermore, he bestowed fine and exquisite garments, the most supreme treasures, crowns and necklaces, bedding, food, drink, and so forth upon all sentient beings;

they were enriched and adorned such that their bodies were like those of the Devaputra Candraprabha, while their cities, palaces, towers, pavilions, gardens, and groves were variously embellished like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
"There are seventy-two hundred thousand nayutas of people who constantly reside in this city;

there are two thousand five hundred ministers and two prime ministers—one named Mahācandra and the other named Dharanīdhara—who are handsome in appearance, possessed of pure and profound merit, deep wisdom, lofty talent, and extensive learning, and who constantly transform all sentient beings through the ten wholesome paths of action."
At that time, during the night while he was asleep, Mahācandra had a dream:
the king, wearing a celestial crown, turned the color of black smoke, and furthermore, a spirit came before the king’s head, seized the crown, and departed.
Having had this dream, he was filled with anxiety and alarm, fearing some ill omen, and reflected to himself:
"My King is compassionate and bestows gifts upon all; he never denies a petitioner."
"There will surely come a wicked man who begs for the king's head.
Having formed this thought, he immediately fashioned a precious head out of the seven treasures, so that if there should be a beggar, it might be used as a substitute.
At that time, the minister Dharanindhara also had a dream, in which he saw the body of Candraprabha’s son disintegrate into its four limbs;
he immediately summoned a Brahmin to divine whether the dream was auspicious or ominous.
The Brahmin said:
"This dream is most ominous; surely there will come from afar someone to beg for the King's head.
Upon hearing this, Dharaṇīndhara wept with grief and sorrow, thinking:
"How can such a great calamity befall my King?"
At that time, twelve thousand five hundred high-ranking ministers all had the same evil dreams:
banners and streamers fell to the ground, golden drums failed to sound, and they experienced the separation from loved ones, wailing and weeping in grief.
Having had such a dream, they deliberated among themselves, saying:
"If the King meets with misfortune, who will provide salvation for all sentient beings?
How shall we ourselves attain peace and security?"
Then the Devaputra Candraprabha again addressed his minister, saying:
"For as long as my life lasts, I shall give to sentient beings without interruption.
At that time, on Mount Gandhamādana, there was a great Brahmin named Akṣimat, who was intelligent, possessed of much wisdom, and skilled in the arts.

He knew that the Devaputra Candraprabha had opened great assemblies for almsgiving at the four gates of the city, beating drums to proclaim his decree and announcing it throughout the four quarters, providing for all who sought aid so that none lacked anything.
"I shall now go there to beg for the king's head.
Having spoken these words, he descended from Mount Gandhamādana.
A celestial being on the mountain, knowing that the brahmin had come to beg for the king's head, lamented with deep sorrow and grief:
"Alas, alas! This king harbors compassion in his heart and seeks the benefit and happiness of all living beings;
if he were to pass away, the world would be deprived of its blessings."

When these words were spoken, heaven and earth grew dark and gloomy; the sun and moon did not appear; springs and wells went dry; a violent wind suddenly arose, blowing sand and driving stones; trees were broken and shattered; and the great earth shook violently—such were the signs of ill omen.

"Not far from the city, there is a seer named Miśraka-mitra who possesses the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Together with five hundred followers, he constantly protects sentient beings with compassion. Seeing these omens, he was deeply distressed and said to his young disciple (*māṇavaka*):
'A calamity must surely be approaching the Sovereign of Men; how shall we provide protection? "
In the void, the hosts of kinnaras and all the devas shed tears like falling fine rain;
all the people were filled with fear and trepidation.
At that time, as the Brahmin Durdarśana was about to arrive at the city, a deva who protected the city approached King Candraprabha and said:
"There is now an evil man coming from Mount Gandhamādana; harboring a murderous intent, he wishes to beg for the king's head. You must not grant him his request."
"You ought to cherish and protect yourself, and ensure the security of your sacred person.
When the king had heard this, his heart leaped with joy, and he exclaimed:
"Excellent!"
"May I bring the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) to fulfillment.

At that time, the brahmin Evil-Eye entered the royal city; however, the celestial being guarding the gate, seeing that the brahmin’s countenance was hideous and ill-omened, remained outside the gate and would not let him in at all.
At that time, the Devaputra Candraprabha, knowing that he had arrived, did not allow him to enter the city, but immediately informed the minister Mahācandra:
"A brāhmaṇa has come from Mount Gandhamādana and wishes to see me."
"Ensure that the gatekeeper does not obstruct him.
Having received these instructions, Mahācandra informed the heavenly being guarding the gate and immediately ordered him to let the man enter.
Upon seeing him, Mahācandra asked the brāhmaṇa:
"You have come here; what do you seek?

The brahmin replied, "I have heard that the Devaputra Candraprabha, out of compassion for sentient beings, has established a great assembly of giving, and that he is not stingy with anything one might request."
"Having come here now, I wish to beg for the king's head.
Mahācandra replied, "Brāhmaṇa!"
"A king's head is composed of pus and blood and will ultimately rot and decay; what use would you have for one obtained through begging?

I possess heads made of the seven treasures, as well as various kinds of gold, silver, and precious gems; I shall offer these all to you, so that you and your descendants may enjoy great wealth forever."
The Brahmin said,
"I originally begged for my head, not for its preciousness.
At that time, the two ministers wept with tears falling like rain, overcome by grief and distress.
"How may we escape this calamity?
At that time, the brahmin went before the king; having seen him, he prostrated himself, stood to one side, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
"I have heard that Your Majesty is compassionate and bestows gifts upon all."
"I have come from afar for this sole purpose: to beg for the King's head.
I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and joyfully grant this gift.
Then he spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva, aspiring for unsurpassed wisdom, Dwells securely in the most supreme and pure Dharma;
I pray you will compassionately grant me your favor and quickly relinquish your head, So as to fulfill the perfection of the pāramitā of dāna.”
Then the Devaputra Candraprabha rose, joined his palms, and spoke in verse:
“This impure body born of my parents— You seek my head and joyfully give it;
May you fulfill your original vow and return with a contented heart, And may I swiftly attain the fruit of Bodhi.”
Having spoken this verse, he said to the Brahmin:
"Do not disdain my head—its marrow, pus, and blood, its skin and flesh joined together, and its lack of purity—but give it to me immediately, so that your original vow may be fulfilled."
At that time, the brahmin was filled with great joy.
When the king wished to cut off his head, he immediately removed his crown;
at that moment, all the crowns throughout Jambudvīpa fell to the ground, and everyone was struck with alarm.
The two ministers, unable to bear seeing the king cast away his life, immediately ended their own lives in that very place;
by the power of their roots of goodness, they were reborn in the palace of Mahābrahmā.
At that time, the yakṣa Pāpaka cried out in a loud voice from the midst of the sky:
"Alas, O Devaputra!
Your life is now coming to an end!"
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of billions of people rushed to the royal palace, weeping and shedding tears, grieving over the pain of separation from those they loved.
The King immediately preached the Dharma to comfort them, causing them to resolve to cultivate the Bodhi-mind.
The Brahmin said,
"If Your Majesty would give up your head, it should be done in a pure place.
The King then replied:
"I have a garden named Maṇiratnagarbha, where flowers and fruits flourish and flowing springs and bathing pools abound; adorned in every way, it is the most excellent of all."
“Regarding this sacrifice of your head, what do you think?
The brāhmaṇa replied,
“I should go there at once.”
The king immediately took his sword and went into that garden; standing beneath a campaka tree, he addressed the brahmin, saying:
"I now relinquish my head; come and cut it off."
The brahmin said, "It is not an act of giving for you to command me to take up the blade while you do not cut it yourself.
At that time, a deva who protected the garden witnessed this event; weeping with tears streaming down his face, he said to the brahmin:
"You great evildoer! The Deva Candraprabha is compassionate toward all and brings universal benefit to living beings.
Why is it that you have taken the life of this deva in this place?"
The King said to the celestial being:
"Do not speak such words to obstruct this supreme matter.

Throughout immeasurable lifetimes in the past, when I was a great king, I gave up my head a thousand times within this very grove; at those times, none of the devas or humans ever presented any obstacle."
In the past, by saving a starving tigress and sacrificing your own body and life, you surpassed Maitreya by forty kalpas; at that time, even the devas and humans did not obstruct you.
Today, by giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, you shall likewise obtain supreme benefit.
“Candraprabha, the Devaputra, further addressed the eight classes of devas and nāgas, and all worthy sages:

‘I now relinquish my head, not seeking the status of a Wheel-Turning King, nor seeking rebirth in the heavens, nor seeking the rank of Māra, nor seeking Śakra, nor seeking Brahmā; rather, I seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so that those who have not yet been transformed may turn their minds and receive transformation, those already transformed may swiftly attain liberation, and those who have attained liberation may fully realize nirvāṇa, the ultimate shore.’”

Furthermore, I vow that after my life comes to an end, my relics shall be like white mustard seeds, and a great stupa shall be erected within the Maṇi-ratna-kośa Garden, so that all sentient beings may pay homage and make offerings, and upon seeing or hearing of it, rejoice;
and that after their lives end, they shall all be reborn in the heavens, resolve to attain Bodhicitta, and emerge from the realm of birth and death.
After he had made this vow, the brāhmaṇa said:
"It is truly rare that the King has renounced his internal wealth; in a future age, you shall swiftly attain the Way of the Buddha."
When he had spoken these words, the king tied his hair to a branch of an *aśoka* tree and, seizing a sharp sword, severed his own head.
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and from the midst of the sky, devas and humans proclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Now the Devaputra Candraprabha shall attain Buddhahood.

Furthermore, they rained down *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *mandārava* flowers, as well as the fragrances of aloeswood, powdered incense, and sandalwood, making various offerings;
they then cremated his remains with sandalwood, collected the relics, and erected a stupa each at the Maṇi Garden and at the crossroads, where they made offerings constantly.
All sentient beings of the present and future who walk, stand, sit, or lie within this grove, or who gaze upon, pay homage to, and make offerings before the stupa,
shall, after the end of their lives, be reborn in the six heavens of the desire realm and the Brahma heavens.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The one who was King Candraprabha in the past is now my own self;
the two ministers, Mahācandra and Dharaṇīdhara, are now Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"The Brahmin Duryodhana is none other than Devadatta now.
For this reason and by these causes, he previously requested before the Buddha that he be allowed to enter parinirvāṇa.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they were all greatly delighted; they accepted it with faith, practiced accordingly, prostrated to the Buddha, and withdrew.
The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Candraprabha Spoken by the Buddha
